name: Calf Slicer from Honey Hole
summary: The calf slicer from Honey Hole is a leg compression submission that folds the trapped foot toward the glute while your shin acts as a fulcrum behind the knee, crushing the calf muscle and loading the Achilles tendon.
description: Master the calf slicer from Honey Hole position in BJJ. Complete guide covering compression mechanics, setup sequences, defensive counters, and training safety.
overview:
The calf slicer from Honey Hole exploits the existing inside leg triangle configuration to attack the opponent's calf muscle and posterior lower leg through compression. Unlike the primary heel hook attacks available from this dominant leg entanglement, the calf slicer targets soft tissue by folding the opponent's foot toward their buttock while your shin acts as a fulcrum across the back of their knee joint. The transition from heel hook hunting to calf slicer requires only a grip change from the heel to the foot, making it a natural secondary attack when the opponent successfully hides their heel.

This submission serves as a complementary weapon within the Honey Hole submission chain, typically deployed when the opponent defends heel hook attempts by tucking their heel deep or maintaining strong wrist control against your breaking grip. The inside leg triangle already provides the necessary fulcrum structure positioned across the back of the opponent's knee. By securing the opponent's foot and driving it toward their glute while extending your hips forward, you generate intense compression on the gastrocnemius muscle, soleus, and Achilles tendon simultaneously.

Strategically, the calf slicer adds a compression dimension to the rotational attacks available from Honey Hole, forcing defenders to address threats across multiple planes of movement. It creates compound dilemmas that make the position increasingly difficult to escape. The technique specifically punishes the exact foot positioning opponents adopt to protect their heel from hook attacks, turning their primary defensive posture into a vulnerability that feeds directly into the compression finish.

injury_risks.injury: Nerve damage to peroneal or tibial nerves
injury_risks.recovery_time: Weeks to months, potential permanent numbness

injury_risks.injury: Deep tissue bruising and compartment syndrome
injury_risks.recovery_time: 2-4 weeks, rare cases require emergency surgery

Physical hand tap on partner or mat
Physical foot tap if hands are trapped
Slapping mat with free hand multiple times
release_protocol: Immediately release foot grip upon any tap signal
Remove shin pressure from calf slowly and controlled
Unwrap legs carefully without jerking movements
Allow partner to extend leg naturally before disengaging
Check partner's mobility and sensation before continuing training
training_restrictions: Never apply at competition speed in training
Never spike or jerk the compression
Never hold after tap to finish the position
Always allow immediate tap access with both hands
Prohibited for colored belts below brown belt in most organizations
Never practice on partners with previous calf injuries without explicit consent

variations_and_setups.description: When opponent hides their heel to defend the heel hook, shift your grip from cupping the heel to controlling the top of the foot and ankle. Thread your near arm under their ankle to capture the foot, then fold it toward their buttock while maintaining triangle pressure.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent successfully defends heel hook by hiding heel deep behind their body or in their armpit

variations_and_setups.description: After securing the foot fold, drive your hips explosively forward and slightly upward to maximize compression across the shin fulcrum. This variation uses hip extension as the primary force generator rather than relying on arm strength to fold the foot.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent has strong leg straightening defense and arm-based folding alone is insufficient to complete the compression

variations_and_setups.description: Tighten the inside leg triangle aggressively while simultaneously folding the foot. The combined triangle compression and foot fold creates dual pressure points on the calf and behind the knee, overwhelming the opponent's ability to resist on a single axis.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against larger or stronger opponents where single-axis compression is insufficient for the finish

attacker.name: from Honey Hole Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack with the calf slicer from Honey Hole. Step-by-step compression setup, grip transitions from heel hook, finishing mechanics, and counters to defensive responses.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the calf slicer from Honey Hole requires recognizing when heel hook defense creates an opening for compression attacks. The transition from heel hook hunting to calf slicer involves shifting grip from the heel to the top of the foot while maintaining your inside leg triangle as the compression fulcrum. This attack capitalizes on the opponent's defensive foot positioning, particularly when they hide their heel deep in their armpit or behind their body. The key to finishing lies in controlled, progressive hip drive that maximizes compression across the shin fulcrum, combined with steady foot folding that bends the knee against your triangled leg. Unlike rotational attacks that target ligaments, the calf slicer attacks muscle and tendon tissue, producing a distinct deep compression pain that opponents must respect immediately.
key_principles: Use the existing Honey Hole inside leg triangle as the compression fulcrum rather than creating new leverage points
Control the opponent's foot completely before initiating the fold to prevent leg straightening defense
Drive hips forward to maximize compression pressure through the shin rather than relying on arm strength alone
Maintain inside leg triangle tightness throughout the grip transition and finishing sequence
Apply pressure gradually and progressively because calf tissue tears before the opponent feels maximum pain
Keep perpendicular body alignment to prevent the opponent from rotating out of the compression angle
setup_requirements: Established Honey Hole position with inside leg triangle fully secured around opponent's thigh
Opponent's heel is hidden or defended, making direct heel hook attacks difficult or impossible
Your shin is positioned across the back of opponent's knee creating the fulcrum point for compression
Both hands are free to transition from heel hook grip to foot control for the fold
Hip positioning allows forward drive to generate compression force through the fulcrum

execution_steps.description: Verify your inside leg triangle is tight around the opponent's thigh with your outside leg crossing their hip. Your shin should be positioned across the back of their knee. Do not proceed if the triangle is loose or the opponent is actively extracting their leg.

execution_steps.action: Release heel hook grip and transition to foot control
execution_steps.description: Let go of the heel hook grip and immediately shift both hands to control the top of the opponent's foot and ankle. Thread your near-side arm under their ankle from the outside, cupping the ball of the foot with your palm. Your far hand controls their shin or ankle for stability.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds, must be smooth to avoid telegraphing

execution_steps.description: Pull the opponent's foot toward their buttock, bending their knee against your shin fulcrum. Lock the foot tight against your chest or shoulder, ensuring you have full control of the ankle joint. The foot should be trapped between your arms and torso with no space for extraction.

Squeeze your inside leg triangle to increase the fulcrum pressure behind their knee. This combined with the foot fold creates dual compression points on the calf muscle from both sides. The tighter your triangle, the more effective the fulcrum becomes at concentrating pressure on the gastrocnemius.

Extend your hips forward and slightly upward, driving your shin deeper across the back of their knee while maintaining the foot fold. This hip extension is the primary force generator for the finish, creating a lever that multiplies the compression force across the calf. Your body weight transfers through your hips into the fulcrum point.
execution_steps.timing: 3-5 seconds of progressive pressure in training

execution_steps.description: Maintain steady, increasing compression by continuing to fold the foot while driving hips forward. The finish comes from the combined pressure of the shin fulcrum compressing the calf muscle while the bent knee stretches the gastrocnemius and loads the Achilles tendon. Apply pressure slowly and be ready for an immediate tap, as tissue damage onset is sudden.
execution_steps.timing: 5-7 seconds minimum in training, never rush

common_counters.counter: Explosive leg straightening before fold is complete
common_counters.your_response: Anticipate the straightening by securing the foot fold early and tight against your torso before driving hips. If they begin straightening, pull the foot harder toward their buttock while simultaneously tightening the triangle to maintain the bent-knee position.

common_counters.counter: Hip rotation toward attacker to reduce compression angle
common_counters.your_response: Follow their rotation with your hips, maintaining perpendicular alignment. If they rotate significantly, consider transitioning back to heel hook since rotation may expose the heel. Use your outside leg across their hip to resist rotation.

common_counters.counter: Full guard pull by extracting trapped leg during grip transition
common_counters.your_response: Minimize the grip transition window by releasing heel hook and securing foot control in one fluid motion. If they begin extracting, immediately re-clamp your triangle and return to heel hook hunting rather than forcing the calf slicer on a partially freed leg.

common_counters.counter: Grip fighting to strip foot control before fold completes
common_counters.your_response: Bury the foot deep against your chest or armpit where their hands cannot reach. Use your far hand to control their wrist while your near arm maintains the foot fold. Two-on-one grip fighting is difficult for them when their leg is trapped.

common_errors.error: Attempting calf slicer before establishing stable Honey Hole position
common_errors.consequence: Without stable triangle and hip control, the opponent easily straightens their leg or extracts it entirely, wasting the attack opportunity and potentially losing the position
common_errors.correction: Always confirm your inside leg triangle is tight and your outside leg is driving across their hip before transitioning from heel hook to calf slicer. Position first, submission second.

common_errors.error: Releasing triangle tension when transitioning grip from heel to foot
common_errors.consequence: Loosened triangle allows the opponent to straighten their leg or begin extracting, eliminating both the calf slicer and the heel hook threat simultaneously
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant triangle squeeze throughout the grip transition. Your legs do the holding while your hands change position. Practice the transition until it requires no conscious thought about leg maintenance.

common_errors.error: Using arm strength alone to fold the foot without hip drive
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient compression force to finish the submission, leading to a prolonged struggle where the opponent can work their escape while you fatigue your arms
common_errors.correction: Drive your hips forward as the primary force generator. Your arms secure the foot position, but the finishing pressure comes from hip extension driving the shin fulcrum deeper into the calf. Think of it as a hip movement, not an arm curl.

common_errors.error: Applying compression too quickly or explosively in training
common_errors.consequence: Calf muscle tears and Achilles tendon damage occur before the opponent can tap, causing serious injury requiring weeks or months of recovery
common_errors.correction: Apply compression over 5-7 seconds minimum in training. The calf slicer causes tissue damage very quickly once the compression reaches threshold, and your partner needs time to recognize the pain and tap before injury occurs.

common_errors.error: Losing perpendicular body alignment during the finishing sequence
common_errors.consequence: Angled body position reduces compression force and creates space for the opponent to rotate their hip and relieve pressure, killing the submission
common_errors.correction: Maintain your body at roughly 90 degrees to the opponent's torso throughout the finish. If you feel yourself drifting parallel, reset your angle by adjusting your outside leg and hip position before continuing pressure.

common_errors.error: Telegraphing the transition by looking at the foot or adjusting body position before releasing heel grip
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recognizes the calf slicer setup and preemptively straightens their leg or begins extracting before you can secure the foot fold
common_errors.correction: Make the grip transition smooth and seamless in one motion. Continue threatening the heel hook right up to the moment you switch. The best calf slicers look like failed heel hook attempts until the fold is already secured.

training_progressions.focus: Fulcrum placement and foot fold mechanics
training_progressions.description: Practice the shin fulcrum positioning and foot fold on a non-resisting partner. Focus on finding the exact placement where your shin crosses the back of their knee for maximum compression. Drill the grip transition from heel hook to foot control 20-30 times per session until smooth.

With a cooperative partner, practice the complete finishing sequence from established Honey Hole. Focus on using hip extension as the primary force generator. Partner provides verbal feedback on pressure location and intensity. Never finish past the point of mild discomfort in this phase.

training_progressions.focus: Heel hook to calf slicer flow
training_progressions.description: Practice flowing between heel hook attacks and calf slicer when partner defends the heel. Start with 30% resistance and increase to 60%. Focus on recognizing the moment heel defense creates the calf slicer opening and executing the transition without hesitation.

Positional sparring starting from Honey Hole with partner at 70-80% resistance. Your goal is to finish via heel hook or calf slicer. Partner attempts all standard defenses. Focus on reading defensive reactions and selecting the appropriate attack. Always maintain safety awareness and slow the finish.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the calf slicer from Honey Hole primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The calf slicer primarily attacks the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles of the posterior calf through direct compression against the shin fulcrum, while simultaneously loading the Achilles tendon through forced knee flexion. Secondary stress is applied to the peroneal and tibial nerves running through the posterior compartment of the lower leg. The combined compression and stretch can cause muscle tears, tendon strain, and in severe cases compartment syndrome.

trap: Harmless squeeze — no need to tap

flashcards.question: Your opponent hides their heel deep behind their body to defend your heel hook - how do you transition to the calf slicer?
flashcards.answer: Release the heel hook grip and immediately thread your near-side arm under their ankle from the outside, cupping the ball of their foot. Their heel-hiding posture actually positions their foot perfectly for the calf slicer fold because their knee is already partially bent. Pull the foot toward their buttock while maintaining your triangle tightness, then drive your hips forward to engage the compression. The key is making this transition in one fluid motion so they cannot straighten their leg during the grip change.
flashcards.answer_line: Thread arm under ankle, cup foot

plausible: Keep heel hook grip, then fold
Straighten their leg to expose calf
trap: Open triangle to grab the ankle

flashcards.question: What are the key safety considerations when applying the calf slicer from Honey Hole in training?
flashcards.answer: Apply compression over a minimum of 5-7 seconds, never spike or jerk the fold. Calf tissue tears before maximum pain is felt, so your partner may not realize they are in danger until damage has begun. Always ensure your partner has at least one hand free to tap, and encourage verbal taps since the leg entanglement can limit hand mobility. Release immediately upon any tap signal and check your partner's calf sensation and mobility before resuming. This technique is restricted to advanced practitioners in most organizations.

plausible: Stop only when pain is sharp
trap: Crank fast for a quick tap

flashcards.question: How should you release the calf slicer from Honey Hole after your partner taps?
flashcards.answer: Immediately release your foot grip and stop all hip drive. Slowly remove shin pressure from the calf without jerking. Carefully unwrap your legs from the triangle configuration, allowing your partner to extend their leg naturally at their own pace. Do not rush to reset or disengage before they have confirmed they are okay. Check their calf for pain, swelling, or reduced range of motion before continuing training. If any concern exists, stop training and apply ice.

trap: Yank the leg straight at once

flashcards.question: Your opponent starts straightening their leg during the fold - what adjustment prevents escape?
flashcards.answer: Pull their foot harder toward their buttock while simultaneously squeezing your inside leg triangle tighter to resist the straightening force. Shift your near-side arm to hook deeper under their ankle, using your entire forearm as a lever against their foot. If the straightening is powerful, drive your hips forward aggressively to increase the fulcrum pressure, making straightening painful. If they successfully straighten past the fold point, abandon the calf slicer and return to heel hook attacks since their straightened leg may now expose the heel.

plausible: Hold still and wait them out

flashcards.question: What grip configuration is needed to fold the opponent's foot for the calf slicer finish?
flashcards.answer: Thread your near-side arm under the opponent's ankle from the outside, with your palm cupping the ball of their foot. Your forearm runs along the bottom of their shin, creating a lever arm. Your far hand can grip their shin, ankle, or your own wrist for reinforcement. The foot should be trapped tight against your chest or shoulder with no gap for extraction. This configuration uses your entire arm as a lever rather than relying on hand grip strength alone, which fatigues quickly against resistance.
flashcards.answer_line: Arm under ankle, cup the foot

plausible: Grip the heel like a heel hook

flashcards.question: You have the fold partially completed but your opponent is actively grip-fighting your hands - what finishing adjustment maximizes compression?
flashcards.answer: Bury the foot deeper against your chest or armpit where their hands cannot effectively reach to strip your grip. Use your far hand to control their near wrist, preventing their grip fighting. Then prioritize hip drive over arm pulling, as hip extension generates far more force than they can overcome with grip fighting alone. If their grip fighting is preventing the fold from deepening, tighten your triangle squeeze to increase fulcrum pressure at the current fold depth rather than fighting for additional fold angle.
flashcards.answer_line: Bury foot, drive hips not arms

plausible: Pull harder with the grip hand
Sit up to see their grips
trap: Let go of the foot to re-grip

flashcards.question: What distinguishes the calf slicer submission timeline from the heel hook in terms of when damage occurs?
flashcards.answer: The heel hook causes ligament damage through rotational force, and the damage onset is extremely sudden with minimal warning pain before catastrophic failure. The calf slicer causes progressive tissue compression damage that builds gradually, but the critical distinction is that significant calf muscle tearing can occur before maximum pain is perceived by the defender. The heel hook has a sharper failure point while the calf slicer has a broader damage zone. Both require immediate respect and early tapping, but the calf slicer's deceptive pain curve makes slow application in training absolutely essential.

trap: Ride the pressure until it hurts

defender.name: from Honey Hole Defender
defender.description: Defend against the calf slicer from Honey Hole. Recognition cues, escape techniques, leg straightening defense, and safety protocols for calf and knee protection.
defender.overview: Defending the calf slicer from Honey Hole requires immediate recognition of the grip transition from heel hook to foot control. When the attacker shifts from hunting your heel to folding your foot, you have a brief window to straighten your leg and resist the compression before full mechanical advantage is established. The primary danger lies in the rapid onset of tissue damage once the fold reaches critical depth, making early recognition and explosive response essential. If the fold progresses past the midpoint with the attacker's hips engaged, tapping immediately is the safest response to prevent serious calf muscle tears or Achilles tendon damage. Your defensive strategy must prioritize prevention over late-stage escape, because once the compression is locked, escape attempts risk accelerating the injury.
key_principles: Recognize the grip transition from heel hook to foot control as the earliest warning of the calf slicer setup
Straighten your trapped leg explosively the moment you feel the attacker release your heel and grab your foot
Maintain maximum knee extension to prevent the fold that creates the compression fulcrum
Tap immediately if the fold progresses past halfway with hip drive engaged, as tissue damage is imminent
Use your free leg to push against the attacker's hip and create space for leg extraction
Never fight through significant compression pain, as calf tears occur before peak pain is reached
recognition_cues: Attacker releases heel hook grip and shifts both hands toward the top of your foot or ankle
You feel your foot being pushed or pulled toward your buttock with increasing force
Increasing sharp pressure on the back of your calf where the attacker's shin crosses behind your knee
Attacker begins hip extension or forward drive while maintaining the inside leg triangle
Attacker threads their arm under your ankle from the outside, cupping the ball of your foot

defensive_options.action: Explosive leg straightening to prevent fold completion
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately upon recognizing the grip transition from heel to foot, before the fold passes the initial bend
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the calf slicer from reaching finishing depth, forcing attacker back to heel hook hunting
defensive_options.risk: Straightening may expose your heel for heel hook if attacker transitions back quickly

defensive_options.action: Hip rotation toward attacker to reduce compression angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the fold has partially progressed but attacker has not yet engaged full hip drive
defensive_options.if_successful: Changes the angle of the shin fulcrum reducing compression effectiveness, buying time for further defense
defensive_options.risk: Rotation may tighten the triangle on your thigh and can worsen position if attacker follows your movement

defensive_options.action: Full leg extraction and guard pull during grip transition
defensive_options.when_to_use: During the brief moment when attacker releases heel hook grip before securing foot control
defensive_options.if_successful: Completely escapes both the calf slicer and the Honey Hole position, recovering to closed guard
defensive_options.risk: Requires precise timing during a narrow window; if too late, attacker may have foot secured already

escape_paths: Straighten trapped leg explosively during grip transition and work to extract from inside leg triangle back to Honey Hole bottom defensive posture
Pull free leg to chest and push attacker's hip away to create enough space for full leg extraction, recovering to closed guard or open guard

favorable_outcomes.how: Straighten your leg to prevent the fold and return to standard Honey Hole bottom defense where you can work established escape sequences against heel hook threats
Extract your trapped leg during the attacker's grip transition window and immediately close your guard before they can re-establish the Honey Hole entanglement

common_errors.error: Waiting to see if the calf slicer will be tight before attempting defense
common_errors.consequence: The compression reaches finishing depth while you hesitate, and once the fold is deep with hip drive engaged, escape is nearly impossible and tissue damage begins immediately
common_errors.correction: React the instant you recognize the grip change from heel to foot. The defensive window is 1-2 seconds maximum. Any delay means the fold progresses to a point where your only safe option is tapping.

common_errors.error: Attempting to grip fight the attacker's hands while leg remains bent
common_errors.consequence: Grip fighting with bent knee is fighting the symptom rather than the cause. The attacker's hip drive generates far more force than your hands can resist, and the compression completes while you fight grips
common_errors.correction: Prioritize leg straightening over grip fighting. Your quadriceps are much stronger than your grip and can resist the fold more effectively. Only grip fight as a secondary measure after straightening your leg.

common_errors.error: Resisting through significant compression pain rather than tapping
common_errors.consequence: Calf muscle tears and Achilles tendon damage occur before maximum pain is reached. Continuing to fight through moderate compression pain frequently results in injury requiring weeks to months of recovery
common_errors.correction: Tap early when you feel building compression pressure that you cannot relieve through defensive movement. The calf slicer's pain curve is deceptive. Preserving your training ability is worth more than avoiding any single tap.

common_errors.error: Pulling trapped leg straight back against the inside leg triangle
common_errors.consequence: Linear extraction against the triangle is mechanically impossible and wastes the critical seconds where rotational or straightening defense would be effective
common_errors.correction: Use leg straightening combined with hip rotation rather than straight-back pulling. The triangle prevents linear extraction but cannot resist quadriceps extension as effectively.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the calf slicer is being set up from Honey Hole rather than a heel hook?
flashcards.answer: The key recognition cue is the attacker releasing their heel hook grip and shifting both hands to the top of your foot or ankle area. You will feel the grip change from cupping your heel to controlling your foot with an arm threading under your ankle. Additionally, the attacker may begin driving their hips forward rather than rotating for the heel hook. This grip transition is your defensive window and must trigger an immediate straightening response.
flashcards.answer_line: Grip shifts from heel to foot

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap to the calf slicer from Honey Hole?
flashcards.answer: Verbal tap is the safest and fastest signal because the inside leg triangle entanglement often limits hand mobility. Call out a clear verbal tap the moment you feel compression building that you cannot escape through defensive movement. If verbal tap is not possible, tap the mat or your partner's body repeatedly with your free hand. Do not wait for maximum pain to develop, because significant calf tissue damage can occur before peak pain is perceived. Tap early and often when caught in this submission.

plausible: Wait for peak pain, then tap
Signal the referee to stop it
trap: Rip your leg free with force

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available against the calf slicer from Honey Hole?
flashcards.answer: The primary defense is explosive leg straightening the instant you recognize the grip transition from heel to foot. This prevents the fold that creates the compression. Secondary defense is hip rotation toward the attacker to reduce the compression angle of the shin fulcrum. If these fail, attempt full leg extraction during the grip transition window to recover guard. If the fold progresses past midpoint with hip drive engaged, all mechanical defenses are effectively exhausted and tapping immediately is the appropriate response.

plausible: Sit up and pry the shin off
trap: Stay folded and ride it out

flashcards.question: Your opponent begins folding your foot toward your buttock and you feel increasing calf pressure - what is your immediate response?
flashcards.answer: Fire your quadriceps to straighten your leg with maximum explosive force. Simultaneously push against the attacker's hip with your free leg to create separation. If straightening fails to break the fold within the first second, assess whether the compression is progressing. If the attacker has hip drive engaged and the fold is deepening, tap immediately rather than continuing to fight. The window between manageable compression and tissue damage is extremely narrow with this submission.

plausible: Grab your own foot to block

flashcards.question: Why is the calf slicer from Honey Hole particularly dangerous compared to calf slicers from other positions?
flashcards.answer: The Honey Hole's inside leg triangle creates an exceptionally stable fulcrum that cannot be displaced through normal defensive movement. Unlike calf slicers from open positions where the defender can create space or change the compression angle, the triangle locks the shin fulcrum in place against the back of the knee. Additionally, the Honey Hole already limits escape options before the calf slicer is even attempted, meaning the defender has fewer tools available. The combination of stable fulcrum, limited mobility, and restricted escape paths makes this variant significantly more dangerous than free-form calf slicers.
flashcards.answer_line: Stable fulcrum, no space to move

trap: It's mild — ride it out, no tap

training_progressions.description: Partner establishes Honey Hole and alternates between heel hook attempts and calf slicer transitions. Your goal is to correctly identify which attack is coming by feeling the grip change. Call out the attack type as soon as you recognize it. Drill 20-30 reps per round to build instant pattern recognition.

training_progressions.focus: Explosive leg extension timing and power
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts calf slicer at 40% speed. Practice firing your quadriceps to straighten your leg the moment the fold begins. Focus on timing the straightening to the earliest possible moment in the grip transition. Increase partner speed to 60% as recognition and reaction time improve.

After successfully straightening against the calf slicer attempt, immediately chain into a Honey Hole escape sequence. Practice the full defensive flow: recognize, straighten, create space, extract leg. Partner increases resistance to 70% and can re-attack with heel hooks if straightening exposes the heel.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance defense with tap awareness
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring starting in Honey Hole bottom with partner at 80% resistance. Partner can attack with any submission including calf slicer. Focus on surviving and escaping while maintaining awareness of when tapping is the appropriate defensive choice. Debrief each round to identify recognition delays.
